name: Amaltari
tagline: Tharu and Bote village on Chitwan's western edge
meta_description: Amaltari, Nawalpur: Tharu and Bote homestays, Narayani boat trips, quiet safaris in west Chitwan and Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge, about 7 km south of Kawasoti.
summary: Amaltari is a Tharu village on the western edge of Chitwan National Park, about 7 km south of Kawasoti in Nawalpur district. It runs one of Nepal's best-known community homestays, started in 2013, and is home to Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge. Come for village life, Narayani boat trips and quiet safaris, October to April.
intro: Amaltari sits where the farmland of Nawalpur meets the forests of Chitwan National Park on the west side of the Narayani. From Kawasoti on the East-West Highway it is about 7 km south on a village road, past rice fields, ponds and mud-walled houses, to the edge of the jungle. The Narayani runs a short walk from the last houses, and beyond the fields the park's grassland and sal forest begin. Rhinos sometimes wander out at night to feed on the crops.

The village is mostly Tharu, with Bote families, the traditional boatmen and fishers of the Narayani, and a smaller Musahar community. In 2013, with support from the government and conservation groups, families opened a community homestay. It grew quickly, mostly with Nepali visitors, and was named the best homestay programme in the country by the tourism ministry in 2017. Most homestay guests are Nepali families and school groups, but hosts have welcomed visitors from many countries, and some younger family members speak English.

For international travellers Amaltari offers two very different stays a few minutes apart: a night with a Tharu family in the homestay, or the comfort of Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge, built in the style of a Tharu longhouse. Either way you get quiet park drives on the western side, boat trips on the Narayani and a real village around you. We suggest one or two nights here, combined with Sauraha or Meghauli, between October and April, when the weather is dry and the park fully open.

story.title: A buffer zone village that chose to host
paras: Amaltari's families have lived beside this forest for generations. Tharu farmers cleared land for rice and kept buffaloes; Bote families fished the Narayani and ferried people across it in dugout canoes. When Chitwan National Park and its buffer zone were set up, access to the forest was restricted, and wild animals from the park began raiding crops. Families needed new income that did not depend on cutting grass and wood inside the park, and tourism was one of the few options open to them.

After Nepal introduced homestay rules in 2010, Amaltari saw a chance. In 2013 families opened their homes to visitors under a buffer zone community homestay, with help from the government and WWF. Guests were assigned to houses in turn, so income was shared, and village dance groups began performing for guests in the evenings. Families who had never hosted strangers learned to cook for guests, prepare rooms and present their songs and dances, and the homestay became a source of pride as well as income.

The project grew fast, drawing busloads of domestic tourists on weekends and holidays. Its success has raised hard questions too, about how fairly benefits reach Bote and Musahar families and how much tourism a small village can absorb. For travellers it remains one of the easiest ways to stay with a Tharu family and see a buffer zone village working. If you stay, ask your hosts how the homestay has changed their village; the answers are usually frank and always interesting.

people: Amaltari is mainly Tharu, with Bote families who traditionally fished and ran ferries on the Narayani, and a smaller Musahar community. Tharu families run most homestays, farm rice, maize and mustard, and keep buffaloes and goats. Many young people work as nature guides, dancers and lodge staff. Tharu, Bote and Nepali are spoken.

untold.fact: Amaltari's community homestay was established in 2013 in the buffer zone of Chitwan National Park and was named the best homestay programme in Nepal by the Ministry of Tourism in 2017.
untold.source: Mongabay, June 2019, 'Homestay programs in Nepal's rhino hub'

untold.fact: The Bote of Amaltari are one of the Terai's river peoples, traditionally fishing and ferrying travellers across the Narayani in dugout canoes long before tourism reached the village.
Amaltari lies about 7 km south of Kawasoti, the headquarters of Nawalpur district, on the western side of Chitwan National Park, part of which extends into Nawalpur.

taste.name: Ghonghi curry
taste.text: Ghonghi are freshwater snails gathered from flooded rice fields and ponds, cooked in a thick curry with garlic, chilli and spices, and eaten by sucking the meat from the shell. Amaltari's homestay kitchens make it often; ask your host, and pair it with rice and dhikri.

facts: Tharu and Bote homestays, Narayani, west Chitwan

highlights.title: Homestay with a Tharu family
highlights.text: Amaltari's community homestay rotates guests between family houses. You eat at the family table, help in the kitchen and join the evening dance programme in the village hall. Expect simple, clean rooms rather than hotel comforts.

highlights.title: Boat trips with Bote boatmen
highlights.text: Bote families have run boats on the Narayani for generations. A trip downriver shows crocodiles, river birds and, with luck, wild gharials, with the Chitwan forest on one bank. Trips run in the dry season only, with life jackets.

highlights.title: Quiet west Chitwan safaris
highlights.text: Jeep drives into the western part of the park from Amaltari see far fewer vehicles than the Sauraha side. Rhinos are common, and the grassland and forest edges are good for tiger and gaur. Bring binoculars and a scarf against the dust.

highlights.title: Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge
highlights.text: Built in the style of Tharu longhouses with mud-plastered walls, this lodge on the village edge offers comfortable rooms, naturalist guides and a farm setting. It usually closes for part of the monsoon, so check dates when booking.

highlights.title: Tharu dance evenings
highlights.text: Village dance groups perform the stick dance and other Tharu dances for guests in the cultural hall, with drums and singing, often followed by a simple Tharu supper. Shows last about an hour, and guests are often invited to join the last dance.

how_to_reach.text: Drive west from Narayangadh on the East-West Highway to Kawasoti, about 35 km, then about 7 km south to Amaltari. Total from Narayangadh is roughly 1 to 1.25 hours; from Kathmandu 6 to 7 hours. Local buses run to Kawasoti, with taxis or the homestay's pick-up to the village.
Fly Kathmandu to Bharatpur (BHR), about 20 to 25 minutes, then drive about 1.5 hours to Amaltari. Check current status before you travel; winter fog often delays morning flights.

where_to_stay: Choose between the Amaltari community homestay, where you stay in a Tharu or Bote family home with simple rooms and home-cooked meals, and Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge on the edge of the village, built in the style of a Tharu longhouse with comfortable rooms and full safari programmes. Barauli's women-run cottages are about 15 minutes away. Kawasoti, 7 km north, has basic hotels for budget travellers.
tips: Avoid Nepali public holidays and weekends at the homestay if you want a quiet stay; domestic groups fill it then.
Bring cash; card payments are rare in the village.
Ask for a homestay family that speaks some English, or book with a guide who can translate.
Book Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge early for February and March, and check its seasonal closing dates in the monsoon.
Respect village rules on dress and photography, and ask before entering kitchens and shrines.

experiences.title: Narayani boat trip with Bote boatmen
experiences.summary: Drift down the Narayani with a Bote boatman, whose community has fished and ferried on this river for generations. Watch for crocodiles, gharials, river birds and wildlife on the Chitwan bank. Trips run only in the dry season.
body: The Bote are one of the Terai's river peoples. Their families have fished the Narayani and ferried travellers across it in dugouts for generations, and some still do. A boat trip from Amaltari puts you in the hands of a boatman who knows every channel and sandbank. If you ask, your boatman will tell you how his family fished and how the river has changed in his lifetime; a guide can translate.

The Narayani is wide and powerful even in the dry season. With the forest of Chitwan National Park on one bank and fields on the other, you pass mugger crocodiles basking on sand, egrets, cormorants, kingfishers and ospreys. The Narayani is the main river for wild gharials in Chitwan, and sightings are possible. In winter, ruddy shelducks and other ducks rest on the calmer stretches, and kingfishers dive from branches that hang over the banks.

Trips end at a landing downstream, where a vehicle meets you, or return upstream if conditions allow. Wear a life jacket, sit still and follow the boatman's instructions. Morning trips give soft light; afternoon trips can end with sunset on the water. Bring a hat, sunscreen and a warm layer in winter, and keep cameras in a dry bag. Ask your homestay or lodge to arrange the boat a day ahead.

faqs.q: Who are the Bote people?
faqs.a: The Bote are a small indigenous community of Nepal's central Terai, traditionally fishers and ferry operators on rivers such as the Narayani. Many live in villages near Chitwan, including Amaltari. Today some still fish and run boats, while others farm or work in tourism.

faqs.q: Is the Narayani boat trip safe?
faqs.a: With an experienced boatman and life jackets, yes. Trips run only in the dry season when the river is calm enough. Sit still, keep hands inside the boat and do not stand. Mugger crocodiles live in the river, so do not trail hands in the water or swim.

faqs.q: Can I see gharials on the Narayani at Amaltari?
faqs.a: There is a fair chance. The Narayani is the main home of wild gharials in Chitwan, and they bask on sandbanks in the dry season, especially in the morning. Numbers are small, so sightings are never guaranteed. Bring binoculars and ask your boatman to watch for them.

experiences.title: Jeep drive in Chitwan's western sector
experiences.image_query: Chitwan National Park western sector jeep
experiences.summary: Enter the park on its western side near Amaltari for drives through grassland, riverine forest and sal forest, with fewer jeeps than the Sauraha side and good chances of rhino, deer and gaur. Dawn drives give the best light and the most activity.
body: The western sector of Chitwan, in Nawalpur district, sees only a fraction of the vehicles that use the tracks near Sauraha. Drives from Amaltari cross into grassland and forest along the Narayani, where rhinos graze and gharials and muggers bask on the riverbanks. Drives usually leave at first light and return by late morning, avoiding the heat of midday, with a second drive possible in the afternoon.

Expect rhinos, spotted deer, hog deer, sambar, wild boar and monkeys, with chances of gaur, sloth bear, leopard and tiger. Birdlife is rich, from peafowl and hornbills to fish-eagles and storks. Stops at watchtowers and lakes let you wait quietly for animals to appear. Your naturalist stops for tracks on sandy stretches and listens for alarm calls from deer and monkeys, which often reveal a predator nearby.

Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge runs drives with its own naturalists, and the homestay can arrange jeeps and guides. Bring a scarf against dust, a hat, water and binoculars. Park entry fees are charged per day, and your guide carries the permits. Private jeeps cost more than shared ones but let you set the pace and stay longer at sightings. Dust can be heavy in April.

faqs.q: Can I enter Chitwan National Park from Amaltari?
faqs.a: Yes. Amaltari is on the western side of the park in Nawalpur district, and jeep drives and walks enter from here with licensed guides and park permits. It is quieter than the Sauraha side. Your lodge or homestay arranges permits and guides.

faqs.q: Is the western side of Chitwan good for wildlife?
faqs.a: Yes. The grasslands and riverine forests along the Narayani hold rhinos, deer, gaur and predators, and the Narayani has the park's main gharial population. Fewer vehicles mean calmer animals and more time at each sighting. February to April is the best season.

faqs.q: Do I need to stay at Tiger Tops to do safaris at Amaltari?
faqs.a: No. Homestay guests can book jeep safaris, walks and boat trips through the homestay committee or a local guide. Tiger Tops guests have activities arranged by the lodge's own naturalists. Park entry fees apply either way. Book a day ahead so permits are ready.

experiences.title: A night in an Amaltari family home
experiences.summary: Stay overnight with a Tharu or Bote family in Amaltari's community homestay: help in the kitchen, eat home-cooked food, watch dances in the village hall and wake early for a walk through the fields. It is simple, warm and personal.
body: Arrive in the afternoon and the homestay committee assigns you to a family. Houses range from traditional mud-walled homes to newer brick buildings with guest rooms. Rooms are simple and clean, with bathrooms that vary between houses; ask for an attached bathroom if it matters to you. Many houses keep buffaloes, goats and chickens in the yard, and the day begins early with milking and sweeping. Bring a torch for the night.

In the evening you help prepare dinner, often rice, lentils, vegetables, pickle and a curry of chicken, fish or snails. Then the village gathers at the cultural hall, where young people perform the stick dance and other Tharu and Bote dances. Families often welcome guests with garlands and tika. Join in as much as you like; hosts are pleased when guests try a few steps of the dance.

Next morning, walk through the fields with your host as buffaloes are milked and children leave for school. Breakfast might be tea, beaten rice and curry or dhikri. It is a short stay but a real glimpse of a Terai village. If you would like to give more than your payment, ask your guide or the homestay committee how to support the village school or community projects.

faqs.q: How does the Amaltari homestay work?
faqs.a: Guests book through the homestay committee or a tour operator and are assigned to a family. Meals, dance programmes and some activities are included or priced by the committee. Income is shared across participating households, and part goes to community funds.

faqs.q: Is Amaltari homestay busy?
faqs.a: It can be, especially on Nepali holidays and weekends, when domestic groups visit. For a quieter stay, come midweek and avoid big festivals such as Dashain and Tihar. International guests are usually placed with families who have hosted foreigners before.

faqs.q: Are Amaltari homestays clean and comfortable?
faqs.a: Rooms are simple but generally clean, with beds, mosquito nets and fans. Bathrooms differ between houses; some are attached and some shared. Hot water may come from a solar heater or bucket. If you want more comfort, stay at Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge and visit the village by day.

experiences.title: Tharu feast and dance evening
experiences.summary: An evening of Tharu food and dance in Amaltari: a thali of rice, lentils, greens, ghonghi snails or river fish and steamed dhikri, followed by the stick dance and women's dances in the village hall.
body: Tharu feasts centre on rice, but the side dishes make the meal. Expect lentils, seasonal greens, a sharp tomato or radish pickle, and a curry of chicken, pork, river fish or ghonghi snails. On feast days women steam dhikri, rice-flour dough rolled into long shapes, and serve it with pickle and curry. Meals are served on a large plate, and many people eat with the right hand, though hosts happily provide a spoon.

Your hosts explain which dishes belong to which festival, from Maghi in January to harvest feasts in autumn, and how the snails are gathered from flooded fields. Rice beer may be offered at some homes; it is fine to decline politely. Ask your hosts what they cook for festivals and what they eat on an ordinary day; the answers differ more than you might expect.

After dinner, walk to the village hall for the dance programme. The stick dance is the highlight: rows of young men strike sticks together in fast rhythm to drums and singing. Women's dances, in traditional dress and silver jewellery, follow. Visitors are often invited to join at the end. Tips for the dancers are welcome and support the village dance group.

faqs.q: What is ghonghi?
faqs.a: Ghonghi are freshwater snails collected from rice fields and ponds in the Terai, a favourite Tharu food. They are cleaned, the shell tips cut, and cooked in a spiced curry with garlic and chilli. You eat them by sucking out the meat. They are most common after the monsoon.

faqs.q: Is the Tharu dance programme included in the homestay?
faqs.a: Usually yes; the evening cultural programme is part of the homestay package, though details change. If you stay at Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge, ask the lodge to arrange attendance or a separate performance. Check what is included when you book.

faqs.q: Can vegetarians join a Tharu feast?
faqs.a: Yes. Rice, lentils, greens, pickles and dhikri are vegetarian, and hosts are happy to skip meat if told in advance. Some dishes use ghee. Tell your host or guide about any allergies before the meal is prepared. Spice levels can be adjusted on request.

faqs.q: Where is Amaltari?
faqs.a: Amaltari is a village in Kawasoti Municipality, Nawalpur district, about 7 km south of Kawasoti on the East-West Highway. It lies on the western edge of Chitwan National Park near the Narayani river, roughly 1 to 1.25 hours west of Narayangadh by road.

faqs.q: Is Amaltari homestay good for foreigners?
faqs.a: Yes, with the right expectations. Rooms are simple and some families speak little English, but hosts are welcoming and used to guests. A guide or translator helps a lot. For a quieter visit, go midweek and outside Nepali holidays, when domestic groups fill the village.

faqs.q: What is Tiger Tops Tharu Lodge like?
faqs.a: It is a comfortable lodge on the edge of Amaltari, built in the style of Tharu longhouses with mud-plastered walls. It offers guided park drives, walks, boat trips and village visits with its own naturalists. It closes for part of the monsoon; check dates when booking.

faqs.q: How many nights should I spend in Amaltari?
faqs.a: One or two. One night covers a village walk, a dance evening and a boat trip or drive. Two nights adds a full day in the park. Many travellers combine Amaltari with Sauraha or Meghauli to see more of Chitwan.

faqs.q: How far is Amaltari from Sauraha?
faqs.a: About 60 km by road, which takes roughly 1.5 to 2 hours via Bharatpur, Narayangadh and the East-West Highway. Private transfers are easiest. There is no direct public bus between the two. A private car can stop at Devghat, a short detour near Narayangadh, or at Barauli on the way.

faqs.q: Is Amaltari good for wildlife?
faqs.a: Yes. It is next to the western sector of Chitwan National Park, with rhinos, deer, gaur, crocodiles and predators, and the Narayani's gharials. Fewer jeeps use this side of the park, so drives are quieter. Village fields are sometimes visited by rhinos at night.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Amaltari?
faqs.a: October to April. February to April is best for wildlife, and October to January is cooler. From mid-June to September the monsoon brings heavy rain, high rivers and limited park access, and some lodges close. February and March, after the grass is cut, give the best views of rhinos and other animals.

faqs.q: Can I visit Amaltari as a day trip?
faqs.a: You can visit for a few hours from Meghauli or Barauli, for a boat trip or village walk. From Sauraha it is a long drive for a day. The village is best experienced overnight, when you join dinner, the dance programme and the early morning in the fields.

faqs.q: Who lives in Amaltari?
faqs.a: Amaltari is mainly a Tharu village, with Bote families, traditional boatmen and fishers of the Narayani, and a smaller Musahar community. Families farm rice, maize and mustard, keep livestock and increasingly work in tourism as hosts, guides and dancers. Bote and Musahar families mostly live in their own hamlets nearby.
